title: Legislative districts of Cotabato

{{Short description|none}} {{Use Philippine English|date=March 2023}} {{Use mdy dates|date=March 2023}} {{Politics of the Philippines}} The '''legislative districts of Cotabato''' are the representations of the [[Provinces of the Philippines|province]] of [[Cotabato]] in the [[List of legislatures of the Philippines|various national legislatures]] of the [[Philippines]]. The province is currently represented in the [[House of Representatives of the Philippines|lower house]] of the [[Congress of the Philippines]] through its [[#1st District|first]], [[#2nd District|second]], and [[#3rd District|third]] congressional districts. The provinces of [[South Cotabato]] (including the province of [[Sarangani]] and the [[Cities of the Philippines#Independent cities|highly urbanized city]] of [[General Santos]]), and [[Maguindanao]] (including the [[Cities of the Philippines#Independent cities|independent component city]] of [[Cotabato City|Cotabato]]) and [[Sultan Kudarat]] last formed part of the province's representation in 1967 and 1972, respectively. Since 2022, the legislative districts excludes municipalities from the [[Special Geographic Area]] of [[Bangsamoro]]. == History == {{further|Legislative district of Mindanao and Sulu}} === Prior to partition of Cotabato Province in 1966 === Initially being excluded from representation in the [[Philippine Assembly|lower house]] of the [[Philippine Legislature]] in 1907, the then-non-Christian-majority areas of the Philippines — which included the [[Department of Mindanao and Sulu]], of which the [[Cotabato (historical province)|undivided province of Cotabato]] was part — were finally extended legislative representation with the passage of the [[Jones Law (Philippines)|Philippine Autonomy Act]] in 1916 by the [[United States Congress]]. The Revised Administrative Code (Act No. 2711) enacted on March 10, 1917, further elaborated on the manner by which these areas would be represented.{{cite book|author=Philippine Legislature|title=Revised Administrative Code of the Philippine Islands of 1917 (Act No. 2711)|date=1917|publisher=Bureau of Printing|url=https://archive.org/stream/RevisedAdministrativeCodeOfThePhilippineIslandsOf1917/Revised%20Administrative%20Code%20of%20the%20Philippine%20Islands%20of%201917#page/n43/mode/2up|access-date=February 5, 2017|format=Digitized Revised Administrative Code of the Philippine Islands of 1917 from the Presidential Museum and Library Collection, uploaded on February 15, 2016}} The non-Christian areas were to be collectively represented in the [[Philippine Senate|upper house]]'s [[Senatorial districts of the Philippines#Twelfth District|12th senatorial district]] by two senators, both appointed by the [[Governor-General of the Philippines|Governor-General]]. Five assembly members, also appointed by the Governor-General, were to represent the seven component provinces of Department of Mindanao and Sulu — [[Agusan (province)|Agusan]], [[Bukidnon]], [[Cotabato]], [[Davao (province)|Davao]], [[Lanao (province)|Lanao]], [[Sulu (province)|Sulu]] and [[Zamboanga (province)|Zamboanga]] — in the [[Philippine Assembly|lower house]] as a [[Legislative district of Mindanao and Sulu|single at-large district]]. These arrangements remained in place despite the abolition of the Department in 1920. It lasted until 1935, when each of the seven provinces was provided one representative to the [[National Assembly of the Philippines]], albeit the manner of election varying between provinces. Voters of the more Christianized provinces of [[Agusan (province)|Agusan]], [[Bukidnon]], [[Davao (province)|Davao]] and [[Zamboanga (province)|Zamboanga]] could elect their representative through popular vote by virtue of Article VI, Section 1 of the 1935 Constitution.{{cite web|author=Commonwealth of the Philippines|title=The 1935 Constitution|date=February 8, 1935|website=Official Gazette of the Republic of the Philippines|url=http://www.officialgazette.gov.ph/constitutions/the-1935-constitution/|access-date=November 19, 2017}} In the [[Moro people|Muslim]]-dominated provinces of [[Cotabato]], [[Lanao (province)|Lanao]] and [[Sulu]], however, voter qualifications were more restrictive: the only persons allowed to vote for the province's representative were past and present municipal officials (municipal president, vice-president, municipal councilors); present senators, assembly representatives and 1935 Constitutional Convention delegates; provincial governors and members of provincial boards; and any persons currently residing in the concerned province who held any of the aforementioned positions in the past.{{cite journal|author=Philippine Legislature|title=Public Laws Enacted by the Philippine Legislature, Acts No. 4203 to 4275|journal=Public Resolutions, Etc |series=Laws, etc |date=1937|publisher=Bureau of Printing Office|page=5|url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=mdp.35112102880830;view=1up;seq=133|access-date=February 5, 2017}} This was the manner by which [[#1935–1967|Cotabato's representative]] was elected in [[1935 Philippine legislative election|1935]]. The [[1st National Assembly of the Philippines]] passed Commonwealth Act No. 44 on October 13, 1936, to finally give all qualified voters of [[Cotabato]] (along with [[Lanao (province)|Lanao]] and [[Sulu]]) the right to elect their [[#1935–1967|own representatives]] through popular vote.{{cite web|author=National Assembly of the Philippines|title=Commonwealth Act No. 44 - An Act applying the General provisions of the Election Law to the election of Assemblymen from the Provinces of Lanao, Cotabato, and Sulu|date=October 13, 1936|website=Official Gazette of the Republic of the Philippines|url=http://www.officialgazette.gov.ph/1936/10/13/commonwealth-act-no-44/|access-date=November 19, 2017}} Voters began to elect their representatives in this manner beginning in [[1938 Philippine legislative election|1938]]. During the [[Second World War]], the undivided Province of Cotabato sent [[#1943–1944|two delegates]] to the [[National Assembly of the Second Philippine Republic|National Assembly]] of the Japanese-sponsored [[Second Philippine Republic]]: one was the provincial governor (an [[ex officio member|''ex officio'' member]]), while the other was elected through a provincial assembly of [[KALIBAPI]] members during the [[Japanese occupation of the Philippines]]. Upon the restoration of the [[Philippine Commonwealth]] in 1945 the province retained its pre-war [[#Lone District (defunct)|lone congressional district]]. Even after receiving its own city charter on June 20, 1959 [[Cotabato City]] remained part of the representation of the Province of Cotabato, per Section 91 of Republic Act No. 2634.{{cite web|title=Republic Act No. 2364 - An Act Creating the City of Cotabato|url=http://laws.chanrobles.com/republicacts/24_republicacts.php?id=2368|website=Chan Robles Virtual Law Library|access-date=February 19, 2017|date=June 20, 1959}} === As the reduced Cotabato Province (1966–1973) === The enactment of Republic Act No. 4849 on June 18, 1966, reduced the territory of Cotabato Province with the separation of its southern municipalities to form the new province of [[South Cotabato]].{{cite web|title=Republic Act No. 4849 - An Act Creating the Province of South Cotabato|date=June 18, 1966|access-date=February 20, 2017|author=Congress of the Philippines|url=http://laws.chanrobles.com/republicacts/49_republicacts.php?id=4853|website=Chan Robles Virtual Law Library}} Pursuant to Section 5 of R.A. 4849, the incumbent representative of Cotabato began to [[#1968–1972|represent only the remaining portion of the province]] (along with the chartered [[Cotabato City|city of Cotabato]]) in the second half of the [[6th Congress of the Philippines|6th Congress]], following the election of South Cotabato's [[Legislative districts of South Cotabato#Lone District (defunct)|separate representative]] in a [[List of special elections to the Philippine Congress#House of Representatives|special election]] held on the same day as the [[1967 Philippine Senate election|1967 senatorial elections]]. === As the current (North) Cotabato Province (1973–present) === On November 22, 1973, the reduced Cotabato Province was further subdivided into the provinces of [[Maguindanao]], [[Cotabato|North Cotabato]] and [[Sultan Kudarat]] by virtue of Presidential Decree No. 341.{{cite web|title=Presidential Decree No. 341 - Creating the Provinces of North Cotabato, Maguindanao and Sultan Kudarat|url=http://www.officialgazette.gov.ph/1973/11/22/presidential-decree-no-341-s-1973/|website=Official Gazette of the Republic of the Philippines|last=Marcos|first=Ferdinand E.|access-date=November 19, 2017|date=November 22, 1973}} All three successor provinces were represented in the [[Interim Batasang Pambansa]] as part of [[Interim Batasang Pambansa#Regional Representatives|Region XII]] from 1978 to 1984. It was during this period that one of them — North Cotabato — was renamed Cotabato through Batas Pambansa Blg. 660.{{cite web|title=Batas Pambansa Blg. 660 - An Act Changing the Name of the Province of North Cotabato to Cotabato|date=March 7, 1984|access-date=February 20, 2017|author=Batasang Pambansa ng Pilipinas|url=http://laws.chanrobles.com/bataspambansa/14_bataspambansa.php?id=660|website=Chan Robles Virtual Law Library}} The present-day (North) Cotabato Province returned [[#1984–1986|two representatives, elected at-large]], to the [[Regular Batasang Pambansa]] in [[1984 Philippine parliamentary election|1984]]. Under the new Constitution which was proclaimed on February 11, 1987, the province was reapportioned into two congressional districts;{{cite web|title=1987 Constitution of the Philippines - Apportionment Ordinance|website=Official Gazette of the Republic of the Philippines|url=http://www.officialgazette.gov.ph/constitutions/the-1987-constitution-of-the-republic-of-the-philippines/the-1987-constitution-of-the-republic-of-the-philippines-ordinance/|author=1986 Constitutional Commission|date=February 2, 1987|access-date=November 19, 2017}} each elected its member to the restored [[House of Representatives of the Philippines|House of Representatives]] starting [[1987 Philippine legislative election|that same year]]. The approval of Republic Act No. 10177 on September 14, 2012, increased the representation of (North) Cotabato by reapportioning the province into three legislative districts.{{cite web|url=http://www.officialgazette.gov.ph/2012/09/14/republic-act-no-10177/|title=Republic Act No. 10177 - An Act Reapportioning the Province of Cotabato into Three (3) Legislative Districts|website=Official Gazette of the Republic of the Philippines|author=Congress of the Philippines|access-date=February 20, 2017|date=September 14, 2012}} The representatives for the newly reconfigured districts were first elected in the [[2013 Philippine House of Representatives elections|2013 elections]]. Despite the reallocation of 63 barangays of Cotabato to the [[Bangsamoro]] in early 2019 (later known as the [[Special Geographic Area]] or SGA), voters in that region are able to vote for local provincial positions including district representatives for the [[2019 Philippine general election|2019 elections]].{{cite news |title=Comelec bars voters of BARMM areas in Cotabato from local polls |url=https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/1537203/comelec-bars-voters-of-barmm-areas-in-cotabato-from-local-polls |access-date=30 November 2024 |work=Philippine Daily Inquirer |date=7 January 2022 |language=en}} However they were barred to do so by the Comelec in the [[2022 Philippine general election|2022 elections]].{{cite news |title=BARMM asks COMELEC to reconsider resolution on SGA polls - BARMM Official Website |url=https://bangsamoro.gov.ph/news/latest-news/barmm-asks-comelec-to-reconsider-resolution-on-sga-polls/ |access-date=30 November 2024 |agency=Bangsamoro Information Office |date=5 January 2022}}{{cite news |title=Fact Sheet: Pros and Cons of Delaying the 2025 BARMM elections |url=https://verafiles.org/articles/fact-sheet-pros-and-cons-of-delaying-the-2025-barmm-elections |access-date=30 November 2024 |date=25 November 2024}} == 1st District == *'''[[Municipalities of the Philippines|Municipalities]]''': [[Alamada, Cotabato|Alamada]], [[Aleosan, Cotabato|Aleosan]], [[Libungan, Cotabato|Libungan]], [[Midsayap]], [[Pigcawayan]], [[Pikit, Cotabato|Pikit]] *'''Population (2020)''': 398,953{{cite web|url=https://psa.gov.ph/sites/default/files/attachments/hsd/pressrelease/2015_Table%201_Legislative%20Districts.xlsx|website=Philippine Statistics Authority|date=2015|title=Population of Population of Legislative Districts by Region, Province, and Selected Highly Urbanized/Component City: 2015|access-date=November 19, 2017}} {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center; width:40%;" |- ! width="40%"| Period !
